entries.title: Project Started:  Global Laundry Alliance (GLA)
entries.description: New project kicked off in the community space.
entries.editedDescription:
Global Laundry Alliance (GLA) is a collaboration reframing access to laundry as a dignity issue and a basic right, not a “nice-to-have” service. It connects communities and organisations working across homelessness, refugee displacement, and global poverty to co-design practical laundry solutions with lived-experience leadership, and to shift the story from charity to systems change.

The project positions laundry spaces as community hubs, using storytelling and shared learning to spread what works across contexts, and build momentum toward policy and funding frameworks that treat clean clothes as foundational to belonging, opportunity, and self-worth.

entries.editedDescription: JusticeHub is a community-owned centre that prototypes practical artefacts and content to strengthen local justice initiatives, with a focus on youth justice and wellbeing. It is built through authentic co-design with Indigenous partners, prioritising community leadership, cultural protocols, and transparent documentation. The goal is to return capacity and value back to local owners through a clear transfer and handover plan, rather than keeping control centralised.

entries.editedTitle: Time in Mount Isa with BG Fit
entries.editedDescription:
Yesterday in Mount Isa, I witnessed the fundamental misalignment at the heart of our community support systems: Those with the deepest community connections often face the greatest barriers to institutional support.

At the local bowling alley, Brodie Germaine a local leader with lived experience of the streets he now serves—was immediately surrounded by young people and parents. Within minutes, ten youth had signed up for tomorrow's fishing trip through nothing more than authentic conversation and established trust. By afternoon, his gym pulsed with energy as young people engaged in purposeful activity.

"People like Brodie are very important," explains Gracie, a police liaison officer. "People that come from a background like these kids, going through the same trauma, same experiences...it gives us a better connection and understanding of the young people."

entries.editedTitle: Launch of the Quandamooka Justice and Healing Strategy
entries.editedDescription:
It was a great honour to be there on The Minjerribah Moorgumpin Elders-In-Council Corporation (MMEIC) officially launched their work towards developing the Quandamooka Justice and Healing Strategy and unveiled our new Justice and Healing hub. Guided by the MMEIC Elders, the justice reinvestment team have been tasked with developing the Quandamooka Justice and Healing Strategy for the region. 

As part of our launch, we they rolled out the community engagement strategy, which means they are now ready to hear from Quandamooka people about what justice and healing means to you and how it can be enacted long-term within the community.

entries.title: Project Started: BCV: Regenerative Conservation
entries.description: New project kicked off in the community space.
entries.editedDescription:
The GP Kits are a set of physical “activation tools” designed to make SMART Recovery easy to refer to from primary care. They use simple, memorable artefacts (notepads, sandtimers, and coasters) to lower the friction for GPs to start a conversation and make a quick referral, helping shrink the typical 12–18 month (or longer) delay before people seek support.

The GPCE Sydney 2024 conference proved the approach works as an engagement and lead-generation channel. Most GPs had low baseline awareness of SMART, but the framing “Do you have a patient with addiction?” landed strongly, and the stall activations (passport comp, drawcards) drove high foot traffic and meaningful conversations. The result was 1,043 kit requests (plus bulk orders and additional partner EOIs, including NZ), making the main “next need” a solid follow-up and fulfilment system to convert interest into ongoing referral pathways.

entries.title: Project Started: AIME
entries.description: New project kicked off in the community space.
entries.editedDescription:
"Every time I go away from here, it's like it's calling me. Come back home," Dianne shared, her words carrying the weight of 23 years living on her traditional lands, beginning with nothing but her car for shelter.

What emerged between A Curious Tractor and this remarkable Traditional Owner wasn't merely a transaction of ideas, but a tapestry of mutual transformation. As Nicholas Marchesi OAM (Him/He) worked alongside Dianne—crafting beds, learning language for the buttons on an "indestructible washing machine"—we witnessed the dissolution of artificial boundaries between "helper" and "helped," revealing instead co-creators of a shared reality.

entries.title: Project Love: The Washing Machine Project
entries.description:
Over 5 billion people still hand-wash their clothes, often in tough conditions. It’s a task that takes time, energy, and health - time that could be spent on education, work, or simply being with family.

These conversations shape the work at The Washing Machine Project. They remind us to listen first, to put people at the heart of everything we design, and to never forget who we’re working for.

entries.editedDescription:
Joe Kwon's journey began in a prison cell. Today, he leads ConFit Pathways, a transformative initiative that uses fitness, mentorship, and lived experience to break the cycle of reoffending among young people.

"In every inmate's life, there are these moments where they're like, I want to do something different," Joe says.

What makes Confit extraordinary isn't just their impressive results in reducing recidivism. It's the powerful premise: every mentor was once incarcerated themselves. They embody the possibility of transformation, turning their darkest chapters into beacons for others.

In detention centres across NSW, Joe and a team of mentors work with young people using what they call the "G Code" - built on gratitude, goal-setting, and groundedness.

"It wasn't the crime that actually got me," Joe reflects. "It was more that belonging, and crime was always that by-factor of wanting to belong to a community because I never felt accepted at school."

This profound insight shapes everything at Confit. When mentors share their journeys, they create authentic connection based on shared experience, meeting young people exactly where they are.

At JusticeHub, we believe the solutions to our most pressing justice challenges already exist in communities. Programs like Confit Pathways demonstrate that when we invest in people-powered initiatives led by those with lived experience, transformation follows.

Our mission is to connect these isolated points of light into a constellation of change. By documenting what works, facilitating knowledge exchange, and supporting visionary leaders like Joe, we're amplifying collective impact and helping successful models scale.

The Confit story represents what's possible when we shift resources from punishment to prevention, when we recognise strength where others see only deficits.

entries.title: Project Started: SMART Connect
entries.description: New project kicked off in the community space.
entries.editedDescription:
We built a culturally appropriate Washing Machine! 

Here is our first crack! "Pakkinjalki kari" (Washing Machine) designed on Warumungu country with the community.

Through hundreds of hours of conversation this is what the community asked for:

- Something that is easy to use // We removed all the buttons and have one "go" button 
- Something that is appropriate for the environment // We hardened all the surfaces with recycled plastic that is easy to clean and durable
- Something this is easy to repair // We built this off one of the most common washing machine's already in market so there are parts and contractors all around the country, however we are creating jobs and businesses by training the community to be able to repair this. 
- Remove the complexity and make the machine smart // We will find this out! 

We have a long way to go as a country in getting desirable, functional and fit for purpose Goods for communities however hopefully this is a step forward. 

So many people to thank along the way but a few

The Warumungu community in particular Dianne Stokes, Norman Frank, Jimmy Frank, Patricia Frank, LT for designing, providing feedback and your cultural wisdom. For trusting us work together, to learn and grow. Thanks Simon Quilty Jimmy Frank Jupurrurla and Wilya Janta for your inspiration and mentorship. 

To Sally Grimsley-Ballard and Georgina Byron AM from the Snow Foundation for your catalytic transformational generosity. If there was Olympics for how philanthropy can accelerate community lead innovation - you would have too many gold medals!

To our design partners Defy Design thank you- Sam Davies you vision, skill and respect for this project, Todd Sidery for your mind, your skills, your energy for this. We are so thankful and excited to keep working together in deep partnership.

entries.editedTitle: NAIDOC Week in Mount Isa with BG Fit
entries.editedDescription:
Watch Brodie Germaine move through his community with a microphone like he's conducting ceremony, not interviews. 

This isn't journalism - it's kinship in action.

Uncle Warren King doesn't mince words about what he sees: 

"This fellow here, I'm very proud of it because he is doing that (passing on culture) as a young man. With his own business and his involvement in community has been staunch strong and resilient as well." 

That's 60,000 years of cultural authority recognising the real thing when it walks past.

Uncle George cuts straight to strategy: 

"It starts with the little kids, you know. You'll see a lot of little kids that walk around the streets... Pull 'em up and have a chat." 

No million-dollar framework. 

Just presence. 

Just care. 

Just the radical act of seeing kids before they disappear.

And Brodie's mother Danielle? 

She drops the wisdom that holds everything together: 

"We just got to keep going, be resilient and not to give up. Even though at times where we think we can't do enough for these kids, we just gotta keep trying so they know that they've got someone there."

1.title: JusticeHub
1.subtitle: TRUTH • ACTION • JUSTICE
1.description: Australia locks up children. Communities have the cure. We connect them. JusticeHub documents 150+ grassroots programs achieving 78% success rates—compared to 15.5% for detention. Indigenous youth are locked up 24x more frequently, costing $1.1M per youth versus $58K for community programs. We're building the infrastructure to redirect resources where they actually work.

quote.text: Communities have always had the solutions. JusticeHub makes them visible, connected, and impossible to ignore.
quote.author: JusticeHub Platform

2.title: Goods.
2.subtitle: Quality Furniture for Every Home on Country
2.description: Every Australian deserves access to quality household essentials, regardless of where they live. Goods on Country partners with Aboriginal Elders and Traditional Owners to deliver durable beds, indestructible washing machines, and essential furniture to remote communities across the NT, WA, and Queensland. 389 assets deployed. Real solutions for real challenges.

quote.text: It took just five minutes to put together, and it's properly comfortable... fellas who'd want something like this.
quote.author: Mark

3.title: CONTAINED
3.subtitle: This costs less. Works better. Already exists.
3.description: A 30-minute experiential installation across 3 rooms that examines youth justice realities. CONTAINED juxtaposes detention ($2,355/day, 84% reoffend) against community programs ($75/day, 88% success). On October 22, 2025, we launch CON|X—infrastructure connecting young people with mentors, employers, and services. Evidence-based alternatives to detention. The data is clear.

quote.text: Every surface designed to eliminate variables that might become hope. We're building something different.
quote.author: CONTAINED
